_comment: Stronger chapters v4 (Ali, 2 Nov): background, the five tests, the badge result leading with the miss. No accessibility or CWV chapter. Copy from the hiring-funnel doc, Copy drafts tab. media values that start with 'file:' are uploaded by seed-stronger-v2.py.

chapters.title: A strong brand with room to test
chapters.caption: strongerlabel.com in September, before the first test went live.
text: Stronger is a Swedish activewear brand that already had a strong design system and good numbers. Joining an existing client with a foundation like that was exciting: I could sit in Figma, reuse their components and try different solutions quickly. Their earlier tests had already shown what works. A view counter on the product page, showing how many people were browsing, had won. Add to cart is the metric Stronger cares about most right now, so I went through the product list and the product page looking for what else could move it.

At TRY, as the frontend between Stronger's e-commerce team and Made People, the agency that runs the storefront. I wrote the test programme, the hypotheses and the GrowthBook setup, designed all five tests in Figma, and built the badge with Made People's team. It shipped inside their senior engineer's merge request.

tests.label: Bestseller badge
tests.title: Bestseller badge on the product list
text: The product list had no signal for what sells. The badge reuses the slot the Archive badge already had in the card's top corner, so the grid never shifts, and follows the colour variant rather than the product family.
tests.caption: Production, same session: the list as shipped, then the variant with "Bästsäljare" on the cards. Under reduced motion the first frame stays.
tests.hypothesis: A bestseller badge is proof of trust, especially for someone buying their first tights. More clicks on the badged cards would lead to more adds to cart and a higher conversion, at the cost of stealing clicks from the other cards. A trade-off I was prepared to pay.
tests.metric: Add to cart rate, target +5 % relative. PLP → PDP click-through as the leading indicator; purchase and revenue guarded.
tests.result: 64,222 users. Bestseller card click 22.5 % → 23.1 % (+2.7 %, 96 % chance to beat control, interval touching zero). PLP → PDP click 48.7 % → 49.4 % (+1.2 %). The other cards gained clicks too (+1.0 %), so the badge did not cannibalise. Add to cart 14.7 % → 14.6 % (−1.1 %, 29 %). Purchase 3.91 % → 3.86 %, flat. Revenue per user −4.5 %, wide interval.
tests.decision: It did not move add to cart. Clicks up, carts flat: hypothesis half-confirmed. Not shipped; the next test goes under the button.

tests.label: Delivery promise
tests.title: One delivery promise, four states
tests.status: Ready · waiting on ops for the cut-off
text: Nothing under the buy button said when an order would ship. One line answers it, and because every state was a component variant, the weekend, holiday and after-cut-off copy surfaced in review before anyone built it. Ready, waiting on ops to confirm the cut-off.
tests.caption: Today's page morphing into the Figma design.
tests.hypothesis: Showing shipping and returns facts under the add-to-cart button lowers hesitation, compared with today, where nothing is shown.
tests.metric: Add to cart, purchase as guardrail. The primary metric is not locked with the client yet.
tests.decision: Ready to build, waiting on ops to confirm the 13:50 cut-off. Runs alongside test 3, on a different part of the page.

tests.label: Sold-out row
tests.title: A row instead of a dead end
tests.status: Designed · exposes on a sold-out tap
text: A sold-out size was a dead end: a notify-me drawer and nothing else, even when the same tights existed in three other colours in that size. The first design redesigned the drawer. In review it shrank to one quiet row under the sizes, shown only when a sold-out size is tapped, which is also the exposure point.
tests.caption: Today's page morphing into the Figma design.
tests.hypothesis: Sending sold-out-size intent to an in-stock colour recovers add to carts that today end in a notify-me form.
tests.metric: Add to cart, purchase secondary. Exposure only on a sold-out tap where another colour has the size, in both arms.
tests.result: Not run yet. Found on the way: the notify-me form said "Skickat!" even when the sign-up failed and sent no events. Flagged as hygiene fixes before the test.
tests.decision: Mobile design and spec done, desktop row still to design. First in the queue after the badge.

tests.label: Similar product
tests.title: One similar product, in your size
text: The same dead end, second answer: when the size is gone in every colour, show one product that has it. Three cards became one. The card is the one that already won a bundle test, and the mapping is hand-picked, so the test measures the idea and not a recommendation engine.
tests.caption: Today's page morphing into the Figma design.
tests.hypothesis: A single, size-matched alternative at the moment of a sold-out tap recovers more add to carts than the notify-me form alone.
tests.metric: Add to cart; purchase and revenue per user secondary. The flag is read in the component that mounts on the tap, so only shoppers who saw the card count.
tests.result: Not run yet. Scoped as an MVP: a hand-picked map of 5 to 10 products, 2 to 3 dev days plus a day of QA.
tests.decision: Designed, specced and estimated. Runs after test 3, never at the same time, since both trigger on the same tap.

tests.label: Kit upgrade
tests.title: Upgrade to the kit, in the cart
text: Forty-seven discounted kits, and the saving only showed on the kit's own page. A shopper with one kit piece in the cart never learned that two more pieces made a kit and saved 248 SEK. The block sits under the matching line, the button is disabled until every size is picked, and one tap swaps the line for the kit.
tests.caption: Today's page morphing into the Figma design.
tests.hypothesis: A shopper who has one piece is more likely to buy the rest of the same kit than unrelated recommendations.
tests.metric: Revenue per exposed user, purchase rate as guardrail. Changed from average order value in review: AOV only counts buyers, so a block that scares off 799 SEK buyers could raise it while losing money.
tests.result: Not run yet. An adversarial review changed six things, among them the metric, kits matched by collection, the price reframed as what you add, and eligibility checked before assignment.
tests.decision: Designed and reviewed. Comes once two kit bugs are fixed: sizes showing as Onesize after a reload, and the free-shipping widget asking for 1 SEK more at exactly 799 SEK.

chapters.title: It did not move add to cart
chapters.caption: Control and variant from production, same session. Badge style GT America 500 12/15 on #18181b.
text: The “Bästsäljare” badge ran on production, 50/50 on a user cookie, about 32,000 users per arm. My hypothesis was that a bestseller badge is proof of trust for someone buying their first pair of tights, that it would pull clicks, and that it would steal some of them from other cards, a trade-off I was prepared to pay. Half of that held. Bestseller cards got 2.7 % more clicks (96 % chance to beat control, interval touching zero), other cards were not cannibalised, and the listing-to-product rate rose 1.2 %. Add to cart, the goal, moved −1.1 %. Purchase −1.5 %, revenue per user −4.5 %, both inside wide intervals. Trust got the click; it did not get the cart.

What I take from it: the badge changed where people clicked, not whether they bought, so the next test belongs where the buying decision is made, under the button. The delivery promise is designed and waiting on the warehouse cut-off; the sold-out-size row and the similar-product card are specced and expose only on a sold-out tap.
